arXiv:2109.07534v1 [math.DG] 15 Sep 2021

Harmonic functions with polynomial growth on manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature

Xian-Tao Huang Address: School of Mathematics
Sun Yat-sen University
Guangzhou 510275
E-mail address: hxiant@mail2.sysu.edu.cn
Abstract.

Suppose (M,g)(M,g) is a Riemannian manifold having dimension nn, nonnegative Ricci curvature, maximal volume growth and unique tangent cone at infinity. In this case, the tangent cone at infinity C⁡(X)C(X) is an Euclidean cone over the cross-section XX. Denote by α=limr→∞Vol​(Br​(p))rn\alpha=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathrm{Vol}(B_{r}(p))}{r^{n}} the asymptotic volume ratio. Let hk=hk​(M)h_{k}=h_{k}(M) be the dimension of the space of harmonic functions with polynomial growth of growth order at most kk. In this paper, we prove a upper bound of hkh_{k} in terms of the counting function of eigenvalues of XX. As a corollary, we obtain limk→∞k1−n​hk=2​α(n−1)!​ωn\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}k^{1-n}h_{k}=\frac{2\alpha}{(n-1)!\omega_{n}}. These results are sharp, as they recover the corresponding well-known properties of hk​(ℝn)h_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). In particular, these results hold on manifolds with nonnegative sectional curvature and maximal volume growth.

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 35A01, 53C23, 58J05.

Keywords: Ricci curvature, harmonic function with polynomial growth, eigenvalue, tangent cone at infinity.

1. Introduction

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a noncompact complete nn-dimensional manifold. Throughout this paper, we always assume n≥2n\geq 2, and the manifold MM will assume to be noncompact and have nonnegative Ricci curvature if not explicitly mentioned. We denote by μ\mu the volume element induced by gg. We fix a point p∈Mp\in M, and denote by ρ⁡(x)=d⁡(x,p)\rho(x)=d(x,p). For a k>0k>0, we consider the linear space

ℋk(M)={u∈C∞(M)∣Δu=0,|u(x)|≤C(ρ(x)k+1) for some C>0}\mathcal{H}_{k}(M)=\{u\in C^{\infty}(M)\mid\Delta u=0,|u(x)|\leq C(\rho(x)^{k}+1)\text{ for some }C>0\}

and denote by hk​(M)=dim​ℋk​(M)h_{k}(M)=\mathrm{dim}\mathcal{H}_{k}(M).

It is well-known that ℋk​(ℝn)\mathcal{H}_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) consists of harmonic polynomials of degree at most kk, and hk​(ℝn)∼2(n−1)!​kn−1h_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\thicksim\frac{2}{(n-1)!}k^{n-1} as k→∞k\rightarrow\infty. See Appendix B of [31] for the details of these facts.

There are many researches on polynomial growth harmonic functions on manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature.

Yau [42] proved that, on complete manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature, any positive harmonic function is constant. In [5], Cheng further proved that on such manifolds any harmonic function of sublinear growth must be constant.

A famous conjecture of Yau says that on a manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) with non-negative Ricci curvature it always holds hk​(M)<∞h_{k}(M)<\infty. Li and Tam solved the case for k=1k=1 and the case n=2n=2 of this conjecture (see [35] [36]). Yau’s conjecture was completely solved by Colding and Minicozzi in [13]. Later on, there are many researches which give better estimates of hk​(M)h_{k}(M).

For example, a more precise upper bound for the dimensions was obtained:

Theorem 1.1 (see [16], [31]).

If (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature, then hk​(M)≤C​kn−1h_{k}(M)\leq Ck^{n-1} for all k≥1k\geq 1, where C=C⁡(n)>0C=C(n)>0 is a constant depending only on nn.

Note that the power n−1n-1 in Theorem 1.1 is sharp compared to the Euclidean case.

There was once a stronger conjecture saying that if (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature, then hk​(Mn)≤hk​(ℝn)h_{k}(M^{n})\leq h_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) holds for every kk. In 2001, Donnelly (see [20]) gave a counterexample to this conjecture. However, there is still an open problem (see e.g. the last question in Section 28 of [32]) on the upper bound of dimensions as follows.

Problem 1.2.

If (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative sectional curvature, then is it true that

(1.1) hk​(Mn)≤hk​(ℝn)\displaystyle h_{k}(M^{n})\leq h_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{n})

holds for every kk?

This problem is unsolved, except the case of k=1k=1 (see [35] and [11]).

One may also ask whether there is a better estimate on the constant CC in the statement of Theorem 1.1, at least under some geometric assumptions on MM.

In [16], Colding and Minicozzi proved that if (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature then

(1.2) hk​(M)≤C1​α​kn−1+C2​f​(kn−1),\displaystyle h_{k}(M)\leq C_{1}\alpha k^{n-1}+C_{2}f(k^{n-1}),

where

(1.3) α:=limr→∞μ​(Br​(p))rn\displaystyle\alpha:=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mu(B_{r}(p))}{r^{n}}

is the asymptotic volume ratio; C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are positive constants depending only on nn; the function f:ℝ+→ℝ+f:\mathbb{R}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+} also depends only on nn and satisfies f⁡(t)≤tf(t)\leq t and limt→∞f⁡(t)t=0\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\frac{f(t)}{t}=0. See Theorem 0.26 in [16].

In [27], the author obtained the following theorem.

Theorem 1.3 (see [27]).

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth, i.e. α>0\alpha>0. Assume the tangent cone at infinity of MM is unique. Then we have

(1.4) limk→∞k−n​∑i=1khi−1=2​αn!​ωn,\displaystyle\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}k^{-n}\sum_{i=1}^{k}h_{i-1}=\frac{2\alpha}{n!\omega_{n}},

and

(1.5) lim infk→∞k1−n​hk=2​α(n−1)!​ωn,\displaystyle\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}k^{1-n}h_{k}=\frac{2\alpha}{(n-1)!\omega_{n}},

where ωn\omega_{n} is the volume of a unit ball in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Remark 1.4.

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature and is collasped, i.e. α=0\alpha=0, then by (1.2), we have limk→∞k1−n​hk=0\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}k^{1-n}h_{k}=0. In particular, (1.4) and (1.5) still hold.

In 1999, Li and Wang have proved a similar theorem, where they assume the manifold having nonnegative sectional curvature, see Theorem 2.2 in [33]. Recall that if a manifold has nonnegative sectional curvature, then its tangent cone at infinity is a unique metric cone. And there are many examples of manifolds satisfying the assumptions in Theorem 1.3 but do not have nonnegative sectional curvature. Also note that we obtain equalities in (1.4) and (1.5), while in [33], the conclusions are some inequalities.

The proof of Theorem 1.3 combines Li and Wang’s proof ([33]), Cheeger-Colding’s theory (see e.g. [8], [9]), some recent development in RCD theory, as well as a theorem on the lower bound of hk​(M)h_{k}(M) (obtained in [19], [26], see Theorem 1.5 below).

A key viewpoint in the proof of Theorem 1.3 is that, for a manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) with nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth, its asymptotically conic property makes the harmonic functions with polynomial growth on it behave like harmonic functions on a cone. This viewpoint has influenced many previous works, see [14], [16], [19], [40], [24], [26] etc.

A natural question is that, under the assumption of Theorem 1.3, can we improve the lim inf\liminf in (1.5) to lim\lim ? The main results of this paper give an affirmative answer to this question. In fact, we will prove some stronger results, see Theorem 1.8 below.

Before we state our main results, we review some work concerning the lower bound of hk​(M)h_{k}(M).

There are manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature on which any harmonic function with polynomial growth is constant, see Theorem 1 in [37] and Corollary 8.12 of [16]. In other words, to ensure the existence of nontrivial harmonic functions with polynomial growth, some additional assumptions on the manifold are necessary.

In Theorem 0.1 of [19], Ding proved that suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature, maximal volume growth and has a unique tangent cone at infinity, then hk​(M)≥C​kn−1h_{k}(M)\geq Ck^{n-1} for some constant CC depending on nn and α\alpha. Note that the power n−1n-1 in this result is sharp compared to the Euclidean case. In a recent paper, Xu obtained the existence of nontrivial harmonic functions with polynomial growth on some manifolds satisfying certain assumptions on its tangent cone at infinity, see Theorem 1.7 in [40]. Note that Xu’s existence theorem does not require the manifold to have maximal volume growth, and an explicit example of a collapsed manifold satisfying the assumptions in Xu’s existence theorem was constructed in [40].

In [19] and [40], the ideas to find nontrivial harmonic functions with polynomial growth are similar. Making use of the conic structure at infinity, we transplant suitable harmonic functions on the tangent cone at infinity back to obtain harmonic functions defined on larger and larger geodesic balls of the manifold. By construction and making use of certain three circles theorems, we can prove these harmonic functions satisfy the desired growth rate. Finally by Arzela-Ascoli theorem we construct a harmonic function with the desired growth rate on the whole manifold. In [40], Xu proved a three circles theorem, which is different from the one given by Ding, see Theorem 3.2 in [40] and Lemma 1.1 in [19] respectively.

Later on, following the ideas of Xu, the author obtained an improved lower bound of hk​(M)h_{k}(M) when MM satisfies the same assumptions as in Xu’s existence theorem, see Theorem 1.2 in [26]. This result recovers Theorem 0.1 in [19] if the manifold has maximal volume growth. In the following, we state the lower bound theorem in the special case that the manifold has maximal volume growth, the more general cases can consult Theorem 1.2 in [26].

Theorem 1.5 (See [19] and [26]).

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature with maximal volume growth. Assume MM has a unique tangent cone at infinity, denoted by (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}), which is an Euclidean cone over the cross section (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). Let 0=λ0<λ1≤λ2≤…0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots be the eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) for the Laplacian operator on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). Let NX:ℝ+→ℤ+N_{X}:\mathbb{R}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{+} be the counting function with respect to (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}), i.e.

(1.6) NX​(λ):=#⁡{i∈ℤ+∪{0}|λi≤λ}.\displaystyle N_{X}(\lambda):=\#\{i\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}\cup\{0\}|\lambda_{i}\leq\lambda\}.

Then given any k>0k>0 such that k⁡(k+n−2)>λ1k(k+n-2)>\lambda_{1},

(1.7) hk≥NX​(β⁡(β+n−2))\displaystyle h_{k}\geq N_{X}(\beta(\beta+n-2))

holds for any positive number β<k\beta<k.

The key point in the proof of Theorem 1.5 is based on the method in [40]: we use L2L^{2}-orthonormal eigenfunctions of the cross section XX to construct as many as possible linear independent harmonic functions with polynormial growth on MM.

Finally we note that in a more recent paper [41], Xu proved another existence theorem provided the manifold satisfies a quantitative strong unique continuation in the sense of Colding and Minicozzi (see [15]).

Now we begin to introduce the new results in this paper.

Theorem 1.6.

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature with maximal volume growth. Assume MM has a unique tangent cone at infinity, denoted by (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}), which is an Euclidean cone over the cross section (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). Let 0=λ0<λ1≤λ2≤…0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots be the eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) for the Laplacian operator on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). Let NX:ℝ+→ℤ+N_{X}:\mathbb{R}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{+} be the counting function with respect to (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) as in (1.6). Then given any k>0k>0, we have

(1.8) hk≤NX​(k⁡(k+n−2)).\displaystyle h_{k}\leq N_{X}(k(k+n-2)).
Remark 1.7.

If we take k>0k>0 satisfying k⁡(k+n−2)<λ1k(k+n-2)<\lambda_{1}, then by (1.8), we have hk=1h_{k}=1. This is a special case of Liouville type theorems proved by Honda (see [24]) and the author (see [26]), where the conclusions hold without the assumption on the uniqueness of tangent cone at infinity. Note that the proof of Theorem 1.4 in [26] is different from the one given in [24], which depending on the maximal volume growth condition. Hence Theorem 1.4 in [26] applies to certain manifolds which does not have maximal volume growth. Motivated by [14], we define some functionals related to a harmonic function on C⁡(X)C(X) in [26], and obtain some good properties of these functionals. In the proof of Theorem 1.4 in [26], given u∈ℋk​(M)u\in\mathcal{H}_{k}(M), we choose parameters carefully to blow down the manifold so that we obtain a harmonic function on C⁡(X)C(X). By the choice of parameters and the good properties of the functionals defined above, we obtain many useful information on uu.

A key in the proof of Theorem 1.6 is a three circles type theorem, see Proposition 4.2. The proof of Proposition 4.2 is based on a modification of that of Theorem 1.4 in [26], where we will show any u∈ℋk​(M)u\in\mathcal{H}_{k}(M) has the desired three circles type property near infinity, and then we apply Xu’s three circles theorem (i.e. Theorem 3.2 in [40]) to uu.

By Theorems 1.5 and 1.6, we have the following corollary.

Corollary 1.8.

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) satisfies the assumptions in Theorem 1.6, with the unique tangent cone at infinity, denoted by (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}). Let NX:ℝ+→ℤ+N_{X}:\mathbb{R}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{+} be the counting function with respect to (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) as in (1.6). Denote by

(1.9) 𝒟X:={β≥0∣β⁡(β+n−2)=λi​ for some eigenvalue λi of (X,dX,mX)}.\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{X}:=\{\beta\geq 0\mid\beta(\beta+n-2)=\lambda_{i}\text{ for some eigenvalue $\lambda_{i}$ of $(X,d_{X},m_{X})$}\}.

Then given any k>0k>0 such that k∉𝒟Xk\notin\mathscr{D}_{X}, we have

(1.10) hk=NX​(k⁡(k+n−2)).\displaystyle h_{k}=N_{X}(k(k+n-2)).

Combining Corollary 1.8 with Weyl’s law on RCD\mathrm{RCD} spaces (see [4] [43]), we have the following corollary.

Corollary 1.9.

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and asymptotic volume ratio α>0\alpha>0. Assume that MM has a unique tangent cone at infinity. Then

(1.11) limk→∞k1−n​hk=2​α(n−1)!​ωn.\displaystyle\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}k^{1-n}h_{k}=\frac{2\alpha}{(n-1)!\omega_{n}}.

Making use of Faulhaber’s formula, one can check that (1.11) implies (1.4). Thus Corollary 1.9 improves Theorem 1.3.

We also prove the following theorem. The conclusion (1.12) is a three circles theorem, which improves Proposition 4.2.

Theorem 1.10.

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) satisfies the assumptions in Theorem 1.6, with the unique tangent cone at infinity, denoted by (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}). Let 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X} be given by (1.9). Suppose k>0k>0 and k⁡(k+n−2)≥λ1k(k+n-2)\geq\lambda_{1}. Then for any u∈ℋk​(M)u\in\mathcal{H}_{k}(M) with u⁡(p)=0u(p)=0, there exists a γ∈𝒟X\gamma\in\mathscr{D}_{X} satisfying γ≤k\gamma\leq k and the followings.

(1):

Given any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists a T=T⁡(M,u,ϵ)T=T(M,u,\epsilon) such that

(1.12) −∫B2​r​(p)u2dμ≤22​γ+2​ϵ−∫Br​(p)u2dμ\displaystyle{\mathchoice{{-\mkern-19.0mu\int}}{{-\mkern-16.0mu\int}}{{-\mkern-16.0mu\int}}{{-\mkern-16.0mu\int}}}_{B_{2r}(p)}u^{2}d\mu\leq 2^{2\gamma+2\epsilon}{\mathchoice{{-\mkern-19.0mu\int}}{{-\mkern-16.0mu\int}}{{-\mkern-16.0mu\int}}{{-\mkern-16.0mu\int}}}_{B_{r}(p)}u^{2}d\mu

holds for any r≥Tr\geq T.

(2):

u∈ℋγ+ϵ​(M)u\in\mathcal{H}_{\gamma+\epsilon}(M) for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

(3):

u∉ℋγ−ϵ​(M)u\notin\mathcal{H}_{\gamma-\epsilon}(M) for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

Remark 1.11.

It is unclear whether (2) in Theorem 1.10 can be improved to u∈ℋγ​(M)u\in\mathcal{H}_{\gamma}(M).

Remark 1.12.

We give some remarks on the connection between Theorem 1.6 and the open problem 1.2. Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative sectional curvature and maximal volume growth, then its tangent cone at infinity is unique. Since the tangent cone at infinity (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)}) is an nn-dimensional Alexandrov space with nonnegative curvature, it is well known that the cross-section (X,dX)(X,d_{X}) is an (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional Alexandrov space with curvature bounded from below by 11. By Theorem 1.6, it is not hard to see that, when the manifolds has maximal volume growth, (1.1) is true provided we can give an affirmative answer to the following long standing open problem:

Problem 1.13.

Suppose (X,dX)(X,d_{X}) is an (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional Alexandrov space with curvature bounded from below by 11, then is it true that

(1.13) λi​(X)≥λi​(Sn−1)\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(X)\geq\lambda_{i}(S^{n-1})

holds for every i≥0i\geq 0?

However, as far as the author knows, except the cases i=0,1i=0,1, there is almost no conclusions on this conjecture, even in the case that XX is a smooth manifold.

Remark 1.14.

The conclusions similar to Theorem 1.6, Corollary 1.8, and Theorem 1.10 still hold provided the manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature and satisfies the followings:

(1):

its tangent cone at infinity with renormalized limit measure is a unique metric cone C⁡(X)C(X) with the unique conic measure of power κ≥2\kappa\geq 2 (see [40] for definitions of these terminologies);

(2):

ℋ1​(X)>0\mathcal{H}^{1}(X)>0;

(3):

there is a positive constant AA such that

(1.14) lim supr→∞μ​(Br​(p))rκ≤A<∞.\displaystyle\limsup_{r\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mu(B_{r}(p))}{r^{\kappa}}\leq A<\infty.

The proofs are almost the same as the ones in this paper. Note that Xu’s example (see Example 4.9 in [40]) is a noncompact manifold satisfying assumptions (1)-(3) and having positive sectional curvature but does not have maximal volume growth.

The conclusions under the assumptions (1)-(3) are related to Question 6.53 and Theorem 6.58 in [16]. We will discuss the relation between them in Section 5. In Section 5 we will also prove an asymptotic dimension estimate similar to (1.11) on collapsed manifolds with nonnegative sectional curvature and satisfying an assumption weaker than assumptions (1)-(3).

Remark 1.15.

The methods in this paper can be applied to prove similar dimension estimates of harmonic functions with polynomial growth on certain RCD⁡(0,N)\mathrm{RCD}(0,N) spaces. For example, conclusions similar to Theorems 1.6, 1.10 and Corollaries 1.8, 1.9 hold on any non-collapsed (in the sense of [17]) RCD⁡(0,N)\mathrm{RCD}(0,N) spaces (Y,d,ℋN)(Y,d,\mathcal{H}^{N}) with α:=limr→∞ℋN​(Br​(p))rN>0\alpha:=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathcal{H}^{N}(B_{r}(p))}{r^{N}}>0 for some p∈Yp\in Y and whose tangent cone at infinity is unique. Here NN is a positive integer and ℋN\mathcal{H}^{N} is the NN-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

2. Preliminaries and notations

In this section, we recall some background concepts on calculus and properties of Ricci limit spaces.

Let (Z,d,ν)(Z,d,\nu) be a complete path-connected metric measure space, equipped with a Radon measure ν\nu. For a locally Lipschitz function f:Z→ℝf:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, denote the pointwise Lipschitz constant of ff by

Lip​f​(x)=lim supd⁡(z,x)→0|f⁡(z)−f⁡(x)|d⁡(z,x).\textmd{Lip}f(x)=\limsup_{d(z,x)\rightarrow 0}\frac{|f(z)-f(x)|}{d(z,x)}.

For f∈L2​(Z)f\in L^{2}(Z), the Cheeger energy is defined by

Ch(f)=inf{fn}{lim infn→∞12∫(Lip(fn))2dν|fn∈Lip(Z)∩L2(Z),∥fn−f∥L2→0}.\textmd{Ch}(f)=\inf_{\{f_{n}\}}\biggl\{\liminf_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{2}\int(\textmd{Lip}(f_{n}))^{2}d\nu\bigl|f_{n}\in\textmd{Lip}(Z)\cap L^{2}(Z),\|f_{n}-f\|_{L^{2}}\rightarrow 0\biggr\}.

The Sobolev space W1,2​(Z)W^{1,2}(Z) is defined as W1,2​(Z):={f∈L2​(Z)|Ch⁡(f)<∞}W^{1,2}(Z):=\bigl\{f\in L^{2}(Z)\bigl|\mathrm{Ch}(f)<\infty\bigr\}. W1,2​(Z)W^{1,2}(Z) is equipped with the norm

‖f‖W1,22:=‖f‖L22+2​Ch​(f).\|f\|^{2}_{W^{1,2}}:=\|f\|^{2}_{L^{2}}+2\mathrm{Ch}(f).

It is known that for any f∈W1,2​(Z)f\in W^{1,2}(Z), there exists |D​f|∈L2​(Z)|Df|\in L^{2}(Z) such that 2​Ch​(f)=∫Z|D​f|2​𝑑ν2\mathrm{Ch}(f)=\int_{Z}|Df|^{2}d\nu. |D​f||Df| is called the minimal weak upper gradient of ff. The minimal weak upper gradient is local in the sense that for any f,g∈W1,2​(Z)f,g\in W^{1,2}(Z), |D​f|=|D​g||Df|=|Dg| holds ν\nu-a.e. on {x∈Z|f⁡(x)=g⁡(x)}\{x\in Z\bigl|f(x)=g(x)\}.

For an open set U⊂ZU\subset Z, we define W1,2​(U)W^{1,2}(U) to be the space of functions f:U→ℝf:U\rightarrow\mathbb{R} locally equal to some function in W1,2​(Z)W^{1,2}(Z) and satisfy f,|D​f|∈L2​(U)f,|Df|\in L^{2}(U). We use Wloc1,2​(U)W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U) to denote the space of functions f:U→ℝf:U\rightarrow\mathbb{R} locally equal to some function in W1,2​(Z)W^{1,2}(Z).

Let U⊂XU\subset X be an open set, then for any f,g∈Wloc1,2​(U)f,g\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U), ⟨D​f,D​g⟩:U→ℝ\langle Df,Dg\rangle:U\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is ν\nu-a.e. defined to be

⟨D​f,D​g⟩:=infϵ>0|D⁡(g+ϵ​f)|2−|D​g|22​ϵ,\langle Df,Dg\rangle:=\inf_{\epsilon>0}\frac{|D(g+\epsilon f)|^{2}-|Dg|^{2}}{2\epsilon},

where the infimum is in ν\nu-essential sense. In the case that W1,2​(Z)W^{1,2}(Z) is a Hilbert space (this holds if (Z,d,ν)(Z,d,\nu) is a Ricci-limit space), the map Wloc1,2​(U)∋f,g↦⟨D​f,D​g⟩∈Lloc1​(U)W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)\ni f,g\mapsto\langle Df,Dg\rangle\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U) is bilinear and symmetric, and we have ⟨D​f,D​f⟩=|D​f|2\langle Df,Df\rangle=|Df|^{2}.

Given an open set U⊂ZU\subset Z, D⁡(Δ,U)⊂Wloc1,2​(U)D({\Delta},U)\subset W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U) is the space of f∈Wloc1,2​(U)f\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U) such that there exists a signed Radon measures μ\mu on UU such that

∫gdμ=−∫⟨Df,Dg⟩dν\int gd\mu=-\int\langle Df,Dg\rangle d\nu

holds for any g:Z→ℝg:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{R} Lipschitz with supp⁡(g)⊂⊂U\mathrm{supp}(g)\subset\subset U. μ\mu is uniquely determined and we denote it by Δ​f{\Delta}f. If U=ZU=Z, f∈W1,2​(Z)∩D⁡(Δ,Z)f\in W^{1,2}(Z)\cap D({\Delta},Z) and Δ​f=h​m{\Delta}f=hm for some h∈L2​(Z)h\in L^{2}(Z), then we say f∈D⁡(Δ)f\in D(\Delta), and denote by Δ​f=h\Delta f=h.

A function f∈Wloc1,2​(U)f\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U) is called harmonic on UU if u∈D⁡(Δ,U)u\in D({\Delta},U) and Δ​u=0{\Delta}u=0 in UU.

For more information on calculus in general metric measure spaces, the readers can refer to [2] [7] [23] etc.

In the following, we assume (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Let ρ\rho be the distance determined by gg, μ\mu be the volume measure determined by gg. Given ri→∞r_{i}\rightarrow\infty, we consider the rescaled metric gi=ri−2​gg_{i}=r_{i}^{-2}g. We denote (Mi,pi,ρi,νi)(M_{i},p_{i},\rho_{i},\nu_{i}), where MiM_{i} is the same differential manifold as MnM^{n}, pi=pp_{i}=p, ρi\rho_{i} is the distance determined by gig_{i}, and νi\nu_{i} is the renormalized measure defined by

νi​(A):=1μi​(B1​(pi))​μi​(A),\nu_{i}(A):=\frac{1}{\mu_{i}(B_{1}(p_{i}))}\mu_{i}(A),

where A⊂MiA\subset M_{i}, and μi\mu_{i} is the volume measure determined by gig_{i}. Then by Gromov’s compactness theorem and Theorem 1.6 in [9], after extracting a subsequence, we can assume (Mi,pi,ρi,νi)(M_{i},p_{i},\rho_{i},\nu_{i}) converges to some (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty}) in the pointed measure Gromov-Hausdorff sense. (M∞,p∞,ρ∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty}) is called a tangent cone at infinity of MM. In general, the tangent cones at infinity may not be unique, that is, it depends on the choice of {ri}\{r_{i}\} and the subsequence. Similarly, the limit measure ν∞\nu_{\infty} may depend on the choice of {ri}\{r_{i}\} and the subsequence.

If (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has maximal volume growth, i.e.

(2.1) α:=limr→∞μ​(Br​(p))rn>0,\displaystyle\alpha:=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mu(B_{r}(p))}{r^{n}}>0,

then by the Cheeger-Colding theory (see [8] [9] [10] etc.) and RCD\mathrm{RCD} theory (see [1] [21] [22] etc.), (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty}) has lots of nice properties.

Firstly, (M∞,ρ∞)(M_{\infty},\rho_{\infty}) is a Euclidean cone over a metric measure (X,dX)(X,d_{X}) with diam​(X)≤π\textmd{diam}(X)\leq\pi, which is denoted by (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)}), with p∞p_{\infty} being the tips. In addition, in this case the limit measure is unique. We have ν∞=1α​ℋn\nu_{\infty}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathcal{H}^{n}, where ℋn\mathcal{H}^{n} is the nn-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

In order to emphasis the cone structure, in the remaining part of this paper, we use the notation (C⁡(X),p∞,dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),p_{\infty},d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}) instead of (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty}).

Secondly, the cross section XX has an induced metric measure structure (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) with mX=1α​ℋn−1m_{X}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathcal{H}^{n-1}, and for any measurable Ω⊂⊂C⁡(X)\Omega\subset\subset C(X), we have

(2.2) mC⁡(X)​(Ω)=∫0∞sn−1​𝑑s​∫Xχ⁡(Ωs)​d​mX,\displaystyle m_{C(X)}(\Omega)=\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{n-1}ds\int_{X}\chi(\Omega_{s})dm_{X},

where Ωs={x∈X∣z=(x,s)∈Ω}\Omega_{s}=\{x\in X\mid z=(x,s)\in\Omega\}, and χ⁡(⋅)\chi(\cdot) is the characteristic function on XX. It is not hard to check ℋn−1​(X)=n​α\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(X)=n\alpha.

Thirdly, (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}) is an RCD​(0,n)\textmd{RCD}(0,n) space, and by Corollary 1.3 of [30], (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) is an RCD​(n−2,n−1)\textmd{RCD}(n-2,n-1) space.

Let ΔX\Delta_{X} be the Laplacian operator on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). Every φi\varphi_{i} always has a Lipschitz representative in the corresponding Sobolev class (see [29]). In the remaining part of this paper, the φi\varphi_{i}’s are always required to be Lipschitz. We also require

for every i≠ji\neq j. By a standard Rellich type compactness Theorem argument, we can derive that λi→∞\lambda_{i}\rightarrow\infty and {φi}i=0∞\{\varphi_{i}\}_{i=0}^{\infty} spans L2​(X)L^{2}(X). Let NX:ℝ+→ℤ+N_{X}:\mathbb{R}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{+} be the counting function defined in (1.6).

Applying Corollary 4.4 in [4] to the RCD​(n−2,n−1)\textmd{RCD}(n-2,n-1) space (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}), we can prove the following result. See Proposition 2.6 in [27] for details.

Suppose (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}) is a tangent cone at infinity of a manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) with nonnegative Ricci curvature satisfying (2.1). Then the following Weyl’s law holds:

hold for any r∈(0,R)r\in(0,R), where ∇(i)\nabla^{(i)} is the gradient with respect to gig_{i}, and DD is the Cheeger derivative with respect to (M∞,ρ∞,ν∞)(M_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty}).

We remark that there is a general theory on convergence of functions defined on varying RCD⁡(K,N)\mathrm{RCD}(K,N) spaces. Except for the notion of uniform convergence, there are other notions of convergence such as (locally) L2L^{2}-weak convergence, (locally) L2L^{2}-strong convergence, (locally) W1,2W^{1,2}-convergence, see e.g. [3]. Theorem 2.4 can be generalized to the RCD⁡(K,N)\mathrm{RCD}(K,N) setting, see e.g. Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.5 of [3].

5. Remarks on the collapsed cases

In this section, we give some remarks on the estimates of hk​(M)h_{k}(M) when MM is collapsed.

As mentioned in Remark 1.14, following the arguments in this paper, we can derive that conclusions similar to Theorem 1.6, Corollary 1.8, and Theorem 1.10 still hold on a manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) with nonnegative Ricci curvature and satisfying assumptions (1)-(3) in Remark 1.14. We omit the detailed proofs. Recall that in [16], Colding and Minicozzi asked, under some assumptions on the tangent cones at infinity on a collapsed manifold MM, are there some improved upper of hk​(M)h_{k}(M) similar but better than (1.2)? See Question 6.53 of [16] for details. Even though assumptions (1)-(3) in Remark 1.14 are more restrictive than the assumptions in Question 6.53 of [16], our conclusions seems better.

In Theorem 6.58 of [16], Colding and Minicozzi proved an improved upper of hk​(M)h_{k}(M) (see (6.59) in [16]) provided (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) have nonnegative sectional curvature and its tangent cone at infinity has Hausdorff dimension mm. Recall that if (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) have nonnegative sectional curvature, then no matter MM has maximal volume growth, its tangent cone at infinity, denote by M∞M_{\infty}, is unique. Furthermore, M∞M_{\infty} is an Alexandrov space with nonnegative curvature with integral Hausdorff dimension m≤nm\leq n; and if m≥2m\geq 2, then M∞M_{\infty} is an Euclidean cone over an (m−1)(m-1)-dimensional Alexandrov space XX with curvature bounded from below by 11; if m=1m=1, then either M∞M_{\infty} is isometric to a line or a half line. Note that if m<nm<n, then in general the renormlized limit measure on M∞M_{\infty} depends on the parameters to blow down MM, see Example 1.24 in [9].

If M∞M_{\infty} is isometric to a line, then MM itself splits. In the case that M∞M_{\infty} is isometric to a half line, then argue as in the proof of Theorem 1.4 of [28], we derive that there is no non-constant harmonic function with polynomial growth on MM.

Thus in the following we always assume m≥2m\geq 2, in particular assumption (2) in Remark 1.14 holds.
